scope.description: Hand-researched deepening pass for English Gym Heroes and five rows that show the first English Gym assembly.

sources.title: Local English WoC release catalog: Gym Heroes
Pokémon TCG API v2 set record: Gym Heroes

claims.text: The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API model Gym Heroes with an August 14, 2000 English release date; Bulbapedia also lists English release date August 14, 2000.
The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API both model 132 Gym Heroes rows for set id gym1.
Bulbapedia describes Gym Heroes as the sixth main English Pokémon TCG expansion and says the Japanese release was Gym Expansion 1: Leaders' Stadium.
Bulbapedia lists Brock, Misty, Lt. Surge, and Erika theme decks for Gym Heroes and frames the set around teaming up with those Gym Leaders.

The local catalog's attention rows include Blaine's Moltres, Misty's Tentacruel, Rocket's Hitmonchan, Rocket's Moltres, Rocket's Scyther, Sabrina's Gengar, trainer portraits, Lt. Surge's Raichu, and Misty deck-linked rows.
The local catalog's credited-artist clusters for Gym Heroes are led by Ken Sugimori, Atsuko Nishida, Keiji Kinebuchi, Sumiyoshi Kizuki, Benimaru Itoh, and Shin-ichi Yoshida.

Gym Heroes matters because it is the first English Gym set: it turns Japanese Leaders' Stadium and related Gym material into an English expansion where owner names, theme decks, and trainer identity become the organizing principle.

not_claiming: English Gym Heroes rows map one-to-one to one Japanese product
steps: Preserve English Gym Heroes / set id gym1 before comparing against Japanese Leaders' Stadium, Japanese theme decks, or W Promotional branches.
Keep owner-name identity intact; do not merge Misty's, Rocket's, Brock's, Erika's, or Lt. Surge's rows into ordinary species rows.
When a card has theme-deck, magazine, or promo lineage, surface that lineage as context rather than treating it as proof of a seller's copy.
For duplicate owner-name species rows, ask for row number and image before importing artist or rarity context.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Gym Heroes is an English assembly of Gym-era materials; agents must keep owner name, row number, and Japanese/source-product lineage visible.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Identifying or comparing English Gym Heroes cards.

narrative.human_title: The first English binder of borrowed teams
narrative.why_it_matters: Gym Heroes is where the English game learns that a Pokémon card can belong to someone. The creatures are familiar, but the ownership changes the air: Brock makes the rocks patient, Erika makes the grass gentle, Surge makes electricity disciplined, and Misty turns water into personality. It is the start of the owner-name grammar that Gym Challenge later sharpens.

sources.title: Local Gym Heroes row: Blaine's Moltres 1
Pokémon TCG API v2 card record: Blaine's Moltres gym1-1

claims.text: The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API identify Blaine's Moltres as Gym Heroes number 1, a Rare Holo Basic Fire Pokémon illustrated by Ken Sugimori.
The Pokémon TCG API records Blaine's Moltres with the attack Phoenix Flame, which costs five Fire Energy and does 90 damage before a coin-flip drawback.
Bulbapedia says Blaine's Moltres was the first card to feature an attack costing five Energy.
Blaine's Moltres matters because the card makes Blaine's identity mechanical: huge flame, huge cost, and a self-resetting drawback, all wrapped around a legendary bird.

not_claiming: all Moltres cards share this energy-cost significance
steps: Preserve the full owner name Blaine's Moltres and row 1 before comparing to ordinary Moltres rows.
Use the five-Energy attack note only for this card's historical context, not as evidence of a seller's copy.
Ask for a clear attack-text image if a buyer specifically cares about Phoenix Flame text or print condition.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Blaine's Moltres is row-specific: its five-Energy Phoenix Flame context should not be applied to generic Moltres cards.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing references Blaine's Moltres, Phoenix Flame, or five-Energy attack history.

narrative.why_it_matters: Blaine's Moltres is wonderfully excessive. Five Fire Energy is not subtle; it makes the card feel like a dare. That is why the owner name works: the legendary bird is not just strong, it has been trained into Blaine's philosophy of all-in flame.

sources.title: Local Gym Heroes row: Misty's Tentacruel 10
Pokémon TCG API v2 card record: Misty's Tentacruel gym1-10

claims.text: The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API identify Misty's Tentacruel as Gym Heroes number 10, a Rare Holo Stage 1 Water Pokémon illustrated by Ken Sugimori.
The Pokémon TCG API records Misty's Tentacruel with the Pokémon Power Flee and the attack Jellyfish Poison.
Bulbapedia says Misty's Tentacruel was released in Japan in the Hanada City Gym Theme Deck and later in Gym Heroes after a Japanese Leaders' Stadium reprint.
Misty's Tentacruel is a perfect bridge from Japanese deck identity to English expansion identity: the same Misty-owned water line gets reassembled from Hanada City Gym into Gym Heroes.

not_claiming: Japanese Hanada and English Gym Heroes prints are interchangeable
steps: Confirm whether the card is Japanese Hanada City Gym, Japanese Leaders' Stadium, or English Gym Heroes before comparing artwork/rarity.
Preserve owner-name and row 10 for the English Gym Heroes card.
Do not treat the Japanese deck origin as proof that a seller's English copy has any particular condition or provenance.
Use Flee / Jellyfish Poison as row confirmation when a listing image is ambiguous.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Misty's Tentacruel crosses Japanese deck and English expansion contexts; agents should keep those assembly layers separate.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing compares Misty's Tentacruel across Hanada City Gym, Leaders' Stadium, or Gym Heroes.

narrative.why_it_matters: Misty's Tentacruel feels like the catalog breathing across products. It starts as a Japanese deck card, passes through Leaders' Stadium, and becomes an English Gym Heroes holo. The card is less a single stop than a little current moving between assemblies.

sources.title: Local Gym Heroes row: Rocket's Scyther 13
Pokémon TCG API v2 card record: Rocket's Scyther gym1-13

claims.text: The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API identify Rocket's Scyther as Gym Heroes number 13, a Rare Holo Basic Grass Pokémon illustrated by Ken Sugimori.
The Pokémon TCG API records Rocket's Scyther with Shadow Images and Blinding Scythe.
Bulbapedia says Scyther did not have an evolution at the time of Rocket's Scyther's release, making the Shadow Images text 'or is evolved' an error.
Rocket's Scyther is a rules-text trap as much as a holo: it carries Rocket ownership and a future-facing evolution phrase that did not yet match the species timeline.

not_claiming: all Scyther cards contain this text issue
steps: Confirm Rocket's Scyther row 13 before applying the Shadow Images error context.
Do not import the 'or is evolved' issue onto ordinary Scyther cards or later Rocket's Scizor cards.
Ask for a clear image of the Shadow Images text if the buyer cares about the error wording.
Keep Rocket ownership visible in search and comparison; do not collapse to generic Scyther.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Rocket's Scyther has a row-specific rules-text error around evolution wording; agents should surface it only after row confirmation.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing references Rocket's Scyther, Shadow Images, evolution wording, or error text.

narrative.human_title: A future evolution hiding in the text
narrative.why_it_matters: Rocket's Scyther is deliciously strange. The card is already evasive in play, then the text gestures toward evolution before Scyther had one in the TCG moment. It is a tiny fossil of the franchise changing under the card frame.

sources.title: Local Gym Heroes row: Lt. Surge's Raichu 28
Pokémon TCG API v2 card record: Lt. Surge's Raichu gym1-28

claims.text: The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API identify Lt. Surge's Raichu as Gym Heroes number 28, a Rare Stage 1 Lightning Pokémon illustrated by Ken Sugimori.
The Pokémon TCG API records Lt. Surge's Raichu with Mega Punch and Thunderbolt, with Thunderbolt discarding all Energy attached to use the attack.
Bulbapedia identifies the Japanese source context for Lt. Surge's Raichu as the Kuchiba City Gym theme deck.
Lt. Surge's Raichu matters because it makes the anime/game Gym Leader bond explicit: a familiar Raichu is no longer generic electricity, it is Surge's disciplined burst of power.

not_claiming: all Raichu cards share Lt. Surge context
steps: Preserve Lt. Surge's owner-name context before comparing to ordinary Raichu rows.
Confirm Gym Heroes row 28 or Japanese Kuchiba City Gym context before importing deck lineage.
Use Mega Punch / Thunderbolt as row-confirming text, not as proof of physical authenticity.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Lt. Surge's Raichu is owner- and product-context specific; generic Raichu comparison is not enough.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing references Lt. Surge's Raichu or a Gym-era Raichu.

narrative.human_title: Surge's electricity has a chain of command
narrative.why_it_matters: Lt. Surge's Raichu is almost austere compared with flashier holos, but that is the charm. It feels trained: Mega Punch, Thunderbolt, all energy spent at once. The owner name turns a mascot evolution into a Gym Leader's instrument.

sources.title: Local Gym Heroes row: Misty's Psyduck 54
Pokémon TCG API v2 card record: Misty's Psyduck gym1-54

claims.text: The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API identify Misty's Psyduck as Gym Heroes number 54, an Uncommon Basic Water Pokémon illustrated by Atsuko Nishida.
The Pokémon TCG API records Misty's Psyduck with Scratch and Call for Friend, which searches for a Basic Pokémon with Misty in its name on a successful coin flip.
Bulbapedia says Misty's Psyduck was first released in the Japanese Hanada City Gym theme deck and that a W Wizards stamped print was included in the August 2000 issue of Top Deck Magazine.
Misty's Psyduck matters because a small character card carries three assembly contexts at once: Japanese deck origin, English Gym Heroes row, and W-stamped magazine promo branch.

not_claiming: unstamped and W-stamped prints are interchangeable
steps: Confirm whether the card is the standard Gym Heroes row, Japanese Hanada City Gym print, or W Wizards stamped Top Deck Magazine print.
If a seller claims W-stamped provenance, ask for a clear image of the W stamp and row details.
Preserve the Atsuko Nishida credit and Call for Friend text as row context, not physical proof.
Do not compare this row only against the earlier Hanada City Gym catalog row without checking language and stamp state.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Misty's Psyduck has Japanese deck, English set, and W-stamped magazine branches; stamp state must be explicit.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing references Misty's Psyduck, W stamp, Top Deck Magazine, or Hanada City Gym origin.

narrative.human_title: The small duck with three doorways
narrative.why_it_matters: Misty's Psyduck is the kind of card that rewards caring. It is not the loudest holo; it is a little connector between Misty's Japanese deck, the English Gym Heroes set, and a magazine-stamped promo branch. The card is a map folded into an uncommon.
